title: Unit 7: Paychecks & Taxes
subtitle: Where your money goes before you see it

questions.prompt: What does 'gross pay' mean on a paycheck?
choices: Your total earnings before any deductions
The money you actually take home
The tax you owe the government
Your yearly bonus
questions.explanation: Gross pay is everything you earned before taxes and other deductions are taken out. It's always the bigger number.

questions.prompt: When deductions come out of your pay, your net (take-home) pay is smaller than your gross pay.
questions.explanation: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions, so it's the smaller amount that lands in your bank account.

questions.prompt: Your gross pay is $1,000 and total deductions are $250. What is your net (take-home) pay?
questions.explanation: $1,000 gross minus $250 in deductions leaves $750 of take-home pay.

questions.prompt: Match each paycheck term to its meaning.
pairs: Form telling your employer how much tax to withhold
questions.explanation: Gross is before, net is after, deductions are what's taken out, and the W-4 sets how much tax gets withheld.

questions.prompt: Which of these are common deductions taken out of a paycheck? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Federal income tax
Social Security & Medicare (FICA)
Your weekly grocery bill
Health insurance premium
questions.explanation: Taxes, FICA, and benefits like health insurance come straight out of your pay. Your grocery bill is spending you handle yourself.

questions.prompt: What is a W-4 form used for?
choices: Telling your employer how much federal tax to withhold from each paycheck
Applying for a credit card
Opening a savings account
Filing for unemployment
questions.explanation: You fill out a W-4 when you start a job so your employer knows how much tax to hold back from each check.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order, from earning money to getting paid.
items: You receive your net pay by direct deposit
questions.explanation: You earn gross pay, taxes and deductions are subtracted, and what's left is deposited as your net pay.

questions.prompt: What is your 'marginal tax rate'?
choices: The rate applied to your last (highest) dollar of income
The rate applied to every dollar you earn
A tax only businesses pay
A flat 10% on all income
questions.explanation: Your marginal rate is the rate on the top slice of your income, not on all of it. Different chunks of income get taxed at different rates.

questions.prompt: Moving into a higher tax bracket means your entire income is suddenly taxed at that higher rate.
questions.explanation: This is the classic 'raise myth.' Only the income above the bracket's threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so a raise always leaves you with more money.

questions.prompt: A tax refund happens when you overpaid taxes during the year and the government returns the extra.
questions.explanation: A refund isn't a bonus. It's your own money coming back because too much was withheld from your paychecks.

questions.prompt: Say the first $10,000 you earn is taxed at 10%, and income above $10,000 is taxed at 20%. If you earn $30,000, how much tax do you owe in dollars?
questions.explanation: 10% of the first $10,000 is $1,000, and 20% of the remaining $20,000 is $4,000, for a total of $5,000.

questions.prompt: You get a raise that pushes part of your income into a higher bracket. What happens to your take-home pay?
choices: Only the portion above the threshold is taxed higher, so you still take home more overall
Your whole paycheck shrinks because you're now 'in' the higher bracket
You take home exactly the same as before
You now owe tax on money you earned in past years
questions.explanation: Brackets are marginal, so a raise always increases your take-home pay. Turning down a raise to 'avoid taxes' never makes sense.

questions.prompt: Match each tax term to its meaning.
pairs: An income range taxed at a set rate
The rate on your last dollar earned
Your average rate across all income
Money back when you overpaid taxes
questions.explanation: Brackets set the ranges, the marginal rate hits your top dollar, the effective rate is your overall average, and a refund returns any overpayment.

questions.prompt: Your effective (average) tax rate is usually lower than your top marginal rate.
questions.explanation: Because your lower income slices are taxed at lower rates, the average you actually pay comes out below your highest bracket rate.

questions.prompt: Sort each example into the type of tax it describes.
items: Tax on the money you earn at your job
Extra amount added at the register when you buy something
Yearly tax based on the value of a home you own
The 8% added to the price of new sneakers
Tax homeowners pay that helps fund local schools
questions.explanation: Income tax hits your earnings, sales tax is added to purchases, and property tax is based on real estate you own.

questions.prompt: What are payroll taxes (FICA) used for?
choices: Funding Social Security and Medicare
Paying for your local library only
Covering your health insurance directly
Repaying your student loans
questions.explanation: FICA taxes come out of your wages to fund Social Security and Medicare, programs that support retirees and people needing care.

questions.prompt: Sales tax is a percentage added to the price of many goods and services when you buy them.
questions.explanation: You pay sales tax at checkout, so a listed price often costs a bit more once tax is added on.

questions.prompt: Match each tax to what it's based on or funds.
pairs: Based on real estate value, funds local services
questions.explanation: Each tax has a different trigger: buying, owning property, earning wages, or earning income overall.

questions.prompt: Which taxes would a teen with a part-time job and no house realistically pay? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Payroll tax (FICA) from their paycheck
Sales tax when they buy things
State income tax in states that charge it
Property tax on a house they don't own
questions.explanation: FICA comes out of every paycheck, sales tax hits purchases, and many states tax wages too. Property tax only applies to real estate you own.

questions.prompt: You buy a $50 item in a place with 8% sales tax. How much sales tax do you pay in dollars?
questions.explanation: 8% of $50 is $4, so the total at the register would be $54.

questions.prompt: Property tax is mainly based on what?
choices: The assessed value of real estate you own, like a house or land
How much you spend at stores each year
The number of hours you work
Your streaming subscriptions
questions.explanation: Property tax is tied to the value of real estate you own, and it usually helps pay for local services like schools and roads.

questions.prompt: What is a 401(k)?
choices: A retirement account offered through your employer, often funded straight from your paycheck
A type of checking account for daily spending
A short-term loan from your boss
A government tax form
questions.explanation: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account. Money can go in automatically from your paycheck, often before taxes.

questions.prompt: An employer 401(k) match is basically free money your employer adds when you contribute.
questions.explanation: If your employer matches your contributions, that's extra money added to your retirement savings just for participating. Not grabbing it leaves free money on the table.

questions.prompt: You contribute $2,000 to your 401(k) and your employer matches 50% of your contributions. How much free money does your employer add in dollars?
questions.explanation: 50% of your $2,000 contribution is $1,000 of employer match, bringing your total to $3,000.

questions.prompt: Match each retirement term to its meaning.
pairs: Free money added when you contribute
Earnings that go on to earn more
questions.explanation: A 401(k) comes from your job, a Roth IRA gives tax-free withdrawals later, the match is free money, and compounding grows your money over time.

questions.prompt: What's a key perk of a Roth IRA?
choices: You pay taxes now, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free
You never pay any taxes ever on any account
Your employer is required to fund it for you
You can withdraw all your earnings with no rules the day you open it
questions.explanation: With a Roth IRA you contribute after-tax money, and later your withdrawals (including all the growth) can come out tax-free.

questions.prompt: Which statements about tax-advantaged retirement accounts are true? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: They let your money grow with tax benefits
An employer match adds free money
You should skip the match to keep more cash today
Starting young gives compounding more time to work
questions.explanation: Tax perks, employer matches, and an early start all help. Skipping the match throws away free money.

questions.prompt: Thanks to compound growth, starting to invest at 22 instead of 32 can build a much bigger nest egg, even with the same monthly contribution.
questions.explanation: Those extra years let your earnings pile up and earn even more, so time is one of your biggest advantages when investing.

questions.prompt: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
choices: Set aside savings or investing money before you spend on anything else
Buy yourself a treat every payday before paying bills
Pay your rent before your savings
Give yourself a raise whenever you want
questions.explanation: Paying yourself first means saving off the top of each paycheck, so saving happens automatically instead of with whatever's left over.

questions.prompt: 'Lifestyle inflation' is when your spending rises as fast as your income, so you never really get ahead.
questions.explanation: Also called lifestyle creep, it's why some people earn more but never save more. Keeping spending steady as income grows is how you build wealth.

questions.prompt: How can splitting your direct deposit help you save?
choices: It automatically sends part of each paycheck to savings before you can spend it
It makes your paycheck arrive faster
It lowers your income tax rate
It doubles your gross pay
questions.explanation: A direct deposit split routes some of every paycheck straight into savings, so you save without having to think about it.

questions.prompt: You take home $1,500 per paycheck and pay yourself first by saving 20%. How many dollars go to savings?
questions.explanation: 20% of $1,500 is $300, moved to savings before you spend the rest.

questions.prompt: Put these 'pay yourself first' money moves in a smart order.
items: Receive your paycheck by direct deposit
questions.explanation: Get paid, save off the top, cover essentials, then spend the rest guilt-free.

questions.prompt: Which are smart money moves at your first job? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Automate savings with a direct deposit split
Grab the full employer 401(k) match
Upgrade your lifestyle to match every raise
Build an emergency fund
questions.explanation: Automating savings, taking the match, and building an emergency fund all set you up. Spending every raise is lifestyle inflation working against you.

questions.prompt: Match each money move to what it means.
questions.explanation: These habits work together: save first, resist creep, automate the split, and keep a cushion for the unexpected.

questions.prompt: Which number on your paycheck is your 'take-home' pay?
choices: Net pay
Gross pay
Your marginal rate
Your bonus
questions.explanation: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions. It's the money that actually lands in your account.

questions.prompt: Your gross pay is $1,200 and total deductions are $300. What is your net pay in dollars?
questions.explanation: $1,200 gross minus $300 in deductions leaves $900 of take-home pay.

questions.prompt: A raise that bumps you into a higher tax bracket taxes your whole income at that higher rate.
questions.explanation: Only the income above the bracket threshold is taxed higher. A raise always leaves you with more take-home pay.

questions.prompt: Your marginal tax rate is the rate applied to which part of your income?
choices: Your last (highest) dollar earned
Every single dollar you earn
Only your savings interest
The money you spend on rent
questions.explanation: The marginal rate hits the top slice of your income, while lower slices are taxed at lower rates.

questions.prompt: Sort each example into the type of tax it describes.
items: Yearly tax based on a home's value
questions.explanation: Income and payroll taxes hit earnings, sales tax is added to purchases, and property tax is based on real estate you own.

questions.prompt: Match each retirement term to its meaning.
pairs: Free money added when you contribute
Earnings that go on to earn more
questions.explanation: A 401(k) comes from work, a Roth IRA offers tax-free withdrawals later, the match is free money, and compounding grows your savings over time.

questions.prompt: You contribute $3,000 to your 401(k) and your employer matches 50%. How much free money does your employer add in dollars?
questions.explanation: 50% of your $3,000 contribution is $1,500 of employer match.

questions.prompt: Which are smart moves with your first paycheck? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Pay yourself first into savings
Take the full employer 401(k) match
Let spending rise with every raise
Automate savings with a direct deposit split
questions.explanation: Saving first, grabbing the match, and automating savings build wealth. Letting spending rise with income is lifestyle inflation.

questions.prompt: An employer 401(k) match is essentially free money, so it's usually worth contributing enough to get all of it.
questions.explanation: The match adds money to your account just for participating, so missing it means turning down free money.

questions.prompt: Put the journey of your money in order, from earning to saving.
questions.explanation: You earn gross pay, taxes and deductions come out, your net pay is deposited, and then you save off the top.
